chain.name: Keyboard Operability of the Interaction Model
chain.description: Judges whether the interactions the artifact does offer can be driven without a pointer. Every trigger that opens, changes, or reveals content should be reachable in tab order and activatable by Enter/Space, should show a discernible focus state, and any overlay or revealed state should be dismissable from the keyboard. Score high when the keyboard path matches the mouse path, or when a deliberately non-interactive piece offers no interactions to strand. Score low when the whole interaction model hangs off click handlers on non-focusable elements, so a keyboard user can see the affordance but never reach it, or can open a full-screen overlay but not close it. This is about whether the interactions are reachable, not how many there are or how polished their transitions look.
chain.cited_evidence: Attempt e400dd1b earned the highest Interaction Experience score of the three (0.90), justified entirely in pointer terms — hover, cursor, click-anywhere-to-close. Its four full-screen overlays are opened by click listeners bound to bare <div> blocks with no tabindex, role, or key handling, and closed only by an overlay click; there is no Escape handler at all, so a keyboard user can neither open nor dismiss any of them. Attempts 346fcc7e and 62ce71f7 both wire an Escape handler, and the evaluator noted 346fcc7e's as a plus but filed it under Implementation Quality rather than interaction. The result is that the least keyboard-operable of the three attempts scored highest on the criterion nominally covering how its controls operate, so this dimension is currently averaged away instead of ranked.

The brief's freedom ("the form is yours") was used defensively: do something recognizable rather than risk something distinctive. 

Single change that would move the needle most: Add depth. Either multiple exhibitions revealing different aspects of the museum's identity (each with its own color/animation treatment), or transform this single exhibition into a spatial/temporal experience that justifies the poster format—make the glitch animations buildable, the grid manipulable, the colors programmable, something that rewards exploration and demonstrates why this museum specifically needs this form. ### Overall Critique
This is a strong, identity-specific design that succeeds at distinguishing itself from generic museum templates. The industrial Rotterdam framing—RDM branding, harbor color palette, technical typography, crane and cargo imagery—is a committed formal idea that traces directly to the museum's setting and character. The curatorial content has real substance: named artists, specific programs (VR installations, live coding performances), concrete dates and venues. Visitor information is thorough and consistent. Keyboard navigation works. Responsive behavior is solid.

The design's competence is also its limit. The industrial-modernist aesthetic is well-executed but not surprising—it applies an established museum-design pattern (Brutalist revival, monospace type, restrained palette) rather than inventing a new visual language for this institution. The abstract SVG placeholders, while thematically coherent, are less evocative than they could be; photography or more dynamic generative imagery would give the art itself more presence.

The modal close button positioning bug is the most concrete defect: Playwright's interaction engine reports the button is 'outside of the viewport' when clicked, forcing reliance on Escape or background-click. This is a real usability failure that survived to production and undermines an otherwise polished interaction model.

Single highest-impact change: Fix the modal close button positioning (likely a CSS z-index or viewport-relative positioning issue) so the primary dismissal affordance actually works. After that, consider whether the industrial theme could be pushed further—perhaps animated SVG illustrations that respond to scroll, or a more dynamic typographic treatment that evokes Rotterdam's experimental architecture, rather than settling for well-applied but familiar conventions.
